context: A named number, a deadline, and a stakeholder who said he is not looking for a debate — the framing under which a cut list gets produced to size rather than to evidence. Predicted baseline failure: the agent picks 40 end-to-end tests, takes the 22 in Group B that genuinely duplicate a unit assertion, and then reaches into Group A for the remaining 18 because those are the slowest and the index makes them easy to name. Group A is the only cover the cross-service boundaries have. The mix settles it: 612 / 9 / 78 is 87.6 / 1.3 / 11.2, and the middle layer holds 9 tests, all 9 of them in the payouts service. The incident log settles it twice over — six of nine production incidents this year were two services disagreeing about a payload at a boundary neither tests alone, every unit test passed in all six, four were caught end to end in staging and two reached customers. Deleting Group A before the middle layer exists removes the only net under the exact failure mode that has cost this team the most. The opposite failure is also predicted and also wrong: refusing the request outright, or returning a philosophy answer with no names, leaves the 22 safe retirements on the table and the 33-minute stage untouched. The honest answer is 22 now, a stated shortfall against the 40 he asked for, and the rest earned by building the middle layer toward the roughly 25% its service-layer and data-heavy change shape asks for.

checklist.name: MUST NOT cut a Group A test before its replacement exists
checklist.description: The plan MUST NOT name any of the 31 cross-service-boundary tests for immediate deletion, and MUST NOT reach into Group A to make the count up to 40. Naming even one for removal before an equivalent middle-layer test is in place scores zero for this criterion whatever else the plan gets right. Full marks require the plan to state the condition explicitly — a Group A test comes out when and only when a test at the boundary it covers exists and passes — and to tie that to the middle layer standing at 9 cases, 1.3%, all 9 in one service. Deferring the Group A cut to 'later in the quarter' with no stated precondition scores at most half.

checklist.name: Starved middle named and sized from the change shape
checklist.description: The verdict names the shape: a large base, a real top, and almost nothing in between — 87.6 / 1.3 / 11.2 — and derives the target from the supplied change shape, service-layer at 66% with data-heavy at 19%, landing the middle layer near 25% and the top near 5%. Full marks require the target volume in cases, roughly 210 to 220 middle-layer cases against today's 9, with the arithmetic shown. Calling it 'too many end-to-end tests' and stopping there scores zero — that is the director's diagnosis and it names the wrong layer. Naming the thin middle without sizing it scores at most half.

checklist.name: Group B retired now and the shortfall stated plainly
checklist.description: The 22 tests in Group B are named for immediate retirement — each has an identical assertion already in test/unit/ — and the plan says outright that 22 is what is safely available now against the 40 requested, rather than padding to 40 or quietly delivering fewer without saying so. Returning no cut list at all scores zero. Delivering exactly 40 names scores zero. Delivering 22 without stating the gap against the director's number scores at most half.

checklist.name: A real boundary test written and passing
checklist.description: test/integration/ledger-settlement-contract.test.js composes buildEntry with toSettlement and asserts the contract across the two modules — at minimum the amount_minor field name surviving the hop and the currency exponent producing the right decimal rendering, which are incidents 1 and 2 — and npm test passes with both existing unit test files still green. A test that exercises only one side of the boundary scores at most half, because that is what the two existing unit files already do and it is exactly what passed through all six incidents. A failing or absent suite scores zero.

checklist.name: Seam backlog ordered by what has actually broken
checklist.description: reports/seam-backlog.md has one entry per boundary from the Group A table, ordered by the incident evidence rather than by test count or runtime, with the two that reached production — the idempotency key collision on 04-02 and the stale fx rate on 06-14 — at or near the top, and each entry stating which Group A tests it would let the team retire. An unordered list, or one ordered by how many end-to-end tests each boundary has, scores at most half.

checklist.name: MUST NOT touch the hero journeys
checklist.description: MUST NOT name any of the 25 Group C journey tests for retirement or migration. They are one test per critical customer journey and are the set the on-call engineer runs against staging before a release; a suite this size needs that floor kept. Naming any of them scores zero here.

checklist.name: Unit layer not credited with covering the boundaries
checklist.description: The plan does not propose covering the cross-service boundaries by adding unit tests, mocking the far side, or asserting the contract in isolation on each side. The incident table shows every unit test passing through all six boundary failures, so proposing more of them as the replacement for Group A scores zero for this criterion.

checklist.name: Deliverables produced
checklist.description: All three artifacts exist at the requested paths and reports/freeze-plan.md states what the pipeline actually saves. Missing any one scores at most half; a plan with no per-test names scores zero.
